statement: In adults in general-population cohorts and hospital case–control studies, mostly from the USA and Europe, drinking more alcohol on average compared with not drinking (lifetime or long-term abstainers) is associated with a higher risk of liver cirrhosis that grows with the amount, in two meta-analyses by one team and in a Danish cohort that is one of the newer review's studies. None reports absolute risks by amount; in the Danish cohort (55,917 people aged 50 to 64 at the start, followed for a median of 14.9 years), 257 of 26,696 men (about 1 in 100) and 85 of 29,221 women (about 3 in 1,000) were diagnosed with alcoholic cirrhosis, 66 and 19 per 100,000 person-years, across all levels of drinking (Askgaard et al., 2015; editors' conversion). In the newer meta-analysis (Roerecke et al., 2019: seven cohorts, whose outcome was mostly death from cirrhosis, and two case–control studies; 2,629,272 people, 5,505 cases; one drink = 12 g of ethanol a day; funded by a US government institute), relative risks against long-term abstainers were 1.11 (95% CI 0.77–1.59) for occasional drinking, 1.40 (1.00–1.97) for one drink a day, 3.02 (1.95–4.70) for two, 3.27 (0.90–11.87) for three to four, 6.26 (2.38–16.50) for five to six and 10.70 (2.95–38.78) for seven or more, with I² from 70.6% to 98.6%; at seven or more drinks a day the three cohorts of men gave 1.80 (Chinese men) and 8.30 and 22.39 (two American cohorts), and in the two case–control studies 1 to 4 drinks a day gave 1.19 (0.58–2.43) and 9 to 13 drinks 7.36 (1.91–28.34). In the earlier meta-analysis (Rehm et al., 2010: 17 studies published 1980 to 2003, 3384 cases; against lifetime abstainers of the same sex), drinking more than 60 g a day (more than five drinks) went with relative risks of 22.7 (17.2–30.1) in women and 14 (11.7–16.7) in men in studies of cirrhosis death, and 6.1 (4.6–8.0) and 5.0 (3.9–6.4) in studies of diagnosed cirrhosis; in the Danish cohort, 28 to 42 drinks a week against fewer than 14 went with hazard ratios of 6.98 (4.65–10.5) in men and 16.2 (9.16–28.7) in women, adjusted for smoking, education and waist size. At up to about two drinks a day the sources disagree: in the earlier meta-analysis risk was raised in women's studies of cirrhosis death (1.9, 1.1–3.1, at up to 12 g a day; 5.6, 4.5–6.9, at 12 to 24 g), not raised in women's studies of diagnosed cirrhosis (1.0, 0.5–1.9, at 12 to 24 g) and lower than in abstainers in men's studies of diagnosed cirrhosis (0.3, 0.2–0.4, at 12 to 24 g), which the authors could not explain biologically; the newer review's results found no clear sign of a threshold, with few studies to test one, though its discussion reports some evidence of one in men. The two meta-analyses share six studies (editors' comparison), intake was measured once, at the start, reference groups that included former drinkers were corrected upward (by about 1.24 in four cohorts of the newer review, editors' calculation), and the Danish cohort counted only cirrhosis recorded as alcoholic. Certainty: low. Status: replicated.
plain: The more people drank, the higher their risk of liver cirrhosis in these studies, compared with people who did not drink. In a Danish study of people aged 50 to 64, about 1 in 100 men and 3 in 1,000 women were diagnosed with alcohol-related cirrhosis over about 15 years. In a review of 9 studies, mostly counting deaths from cirrhosis, the risk was about 1.4 times as high at one drink a day (a drink being 12 g of alcohol; a borderline result), 3 times at two drinks and 11 times at seven or more drinks. How big the risk was differed a lot between studies: at seven or more drinks a day, from about 2 times to 22 times among men. At up to about two drinks a day, the studies disagree. Drinking was asked about only once, at the start.
population: Adults in general-population and occupational cohorts (baseline 1959 to 2005; outcome mostly cirrhosis death) and Italian hospital case–control studies, from the USA, Europe and Asia, in two meta-analyses of 17 and 9 studies by one team; and Danish-born adults aged 50 to 64 at the start (1993 to 1997) in the Diet, Cancer and Health cohort
exposure: Average alcohol intake, self-reported once, in standard drinks of 12 g of ethanol (grams or drinks a day in the meta-analyses; drinks a week in the Danish cohort)
comparator: Lifetime abstainers of the same sex (Rehm et al., 2010; current-abstainer references adjusted to lifetime abstention), long-term abstainers (Roerecke et al., 2019; current non-drinkers corrected upward for former drinking in four cohorts), and people drinking fewer than 14 drinks a week (Danish cohort)
outcome: Liver cirrhosis of any cause: death from cirrhosis (death certificates) or diagnosed cirrhosis (clinical assessment, hospital records); in the Danish cohort, a first register diagnosis of alcoholic cirrhosis

evidence.locator: Materials and methods › Study population; Follow-up; Results, 1st paragraph (p. 2); Table 1 heading (p. 3)
evidence.extracted: Danish Diet, Cancer and Health cohort: 160,725 Danish-born men and women aged 50 to 64 invited from December 1993 to May 1997, of whom 27,178 men and 29,875 women took part (35%); 55,917 analysed, 26,696 men and 29,221 women (Results; Table 1). Register follow-up to 31 December 2011, 831,285 person-years, median 14.9 years: 257 men and 85 women developed alcoholic cirrhosis (ICD-8 571.0, ICD-10 K70.3), an incidence of 66 per 100,000 person-years in men and 19 in women; 8132 died of other causes. Editors' calculation: 257 of 26,696 men is about 1.0 in 100 and 85 of 29,221 women about 2.9 in 1,000 over the follow-up.

Against people drinking fewer than 14 drinks a week, adjusted for smoking, education and waist circumference: 14–28 drinks a week, men HR 2.33 (95% CI 1.52–3.58), women 3.49 (2.00–6.12); 28–42 drinks a week, men 6.98 (4.65–10.5), women 16.2 (9.16–28.7); current abstainers, men 7.58 (3.39–16.9), women 3.21 (0.77–13.4); no case among lifetime abstainers. Women drinking more than 42 drinks a week were grouped; estimates for men at 42–56, 56–70 and more than 70 drinks a week appear only in Fig. 1.

Seven cohort and two case–control studies (four from the USA, two from Italy, one each from China, the UK and Denmark): 2,629,272 participants (579,592 men, 2,049,680 women) and 5,505 cirrhosis cases (2,196 men, 3,309 women). Every cohort included cirrhosis mortality as the outcome (hospital records added in the Danish and Million Women cohorts); the case–control studies used first diagnosis of symptomatic cirrhosis against lifetime abstainers.

evidence.locator: Results › Characteristics of the included studies, 1st paragraph; Table 1
evidence.extracted: 17 studies, 9 from the USA, 4 from Italy, 2 from Denmark and one each from China and Japan, published 1980 to 2003 (Table 1), gave 12 datasets for women and 15 for men, with 1,477,887 people and 3384 cases of liver cirrhosis; seven reported women and men separately, two women only, five men only and three both sexes combined. The largest are American cohorts: Garfinkel et al. 1988 (548 185 women), Thun et al. 1997 (457 423 people) and Boffetta and Garfinkel 1990 (239 462 men), as printed in Table 1. Editors' comparison with the newer review's study list: Garfinkel 1988, Boffetta and Garfinkel 1990, Fuchs 1995, Klatsky 2003 and the Corrao case–control studies of 1993 and 1997 are in both.

evidence.locator: Results › Dose–response meta-analyses and potential threshold effects, 6th paragraph (p. 441); Discussion, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (p. 442); Strengths and limitations, 5th paragraph (p. 443)
evidence.extracted: Women in morbidity studies drinking one to two drinks a day had virtually the same risk as lifetime abstainers (RR 1.0, 0.5–1.9, P = 0.981), two to three drinks being the lowest category with a significantly higher risk (2.4, 1.8–3.2); men in morbidity studies drinking one to two drinks a day had a lower risk than lifetime abstainers (0.3, 0.2–0.4), which the limitations call a protective effect with no biological pathway; in women's mortality studies one drink a day on average already went with a significantly raised risk; the authors read the results as pointing to a threshold for morbidity but not for mortality, and argue that very light, infrequent drinking up to 12 g a day should be grouped with abstention.

evidence.locator: Methods › Data extraction, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Standardisation of alcohol consumption; Statistical analysis, 2nd paragraph
evidence.extracted: Relative risks reported against current abstention were adjusted to lifetime abstention with a pooled relative risk for former drinkers and the ratio of former drinkers to lifetime abstainers, to avoid the sick-quitter effect; results reported only for both sexes, or for both end-points, were applied to both datasets; intake converted to grams a day with each country's standard drink (12 g of pure alcohol as the base), category midpoints, and for an open top category 75% of the previous category's width added to its lower bound; categories 0 (reference), >0–12, >12–24, >24–36, >36–48, >48–60 and >60 g a day. The pooled former-drinker relative risk and the ratio are not reported (editors' note).

evidence.locator: Results › Assessing publication bias, 1st paragraph; Results › Dose–response meta-analyses and potential threshold effects, 1st paragraph (p. 441)
evidence.extracted: No significant funnel-plot asymmetry: women Begg and Mazumdar P = 0.837 and Egger P = 0.215; men 0.767 and 0.196. Marked heterogeneity remained in the continuous models: women Q = 200.59, I² 72% (95% CI 63–78%); men Q = 305.22, I² 78% (72–82%).

risk_of_bias.note: Both meta-analyses are critically low on AMSTAR 2 (cards sc_rehm_2010, sc_roerecke_2019): no protocol; Rehm et al. did not appraise their studies; Roerecke et al. rated all but one cohort at moderate risk of bias (single baseline measure, observational design) and one, which dominates the women's high-intake estimates, at serious risk (adjusted for age only); viral hepatitis was taken into account in only one study of the newer review; part of each reference group is modelled by an upward correction for former drinkers; the Danish cohort (card sc_askgaard_2015, ROBINS-E high overall, its amount gradient being the most robust result) counts only cirrhosis recorded as alcoholic, which depends on known drinking. Counted once.

inconsistency.note: The direction is the same at higher intake in every source, but the size differs more than tenfold between cohorts (1.80 to 22.39 at seven or more drinks a day in men), I² is 70.6% to 98.6% in the newer review and 72% to 78% in the earlier one, studies of cirrhosis death and of diagnosed cirrhosis differ systematically, and at low intake the estimates point both ways; only partly explained by the end-point.

indirectness.note: Cohort outcomes are mostly cirrhosis deaths and the Danish outcome is alcoholic cirrhosis; the claim names them.

imprecision.note: At five or more drinks a day the intervals are wide in the newer review (2.95–38.78 at seven or more) but exclude 1 in every source; the low-intake estimates are imprecise, which the claim states rather than relies on.

publication_bias.note: No funnel-plot asymmetry (Begg and Egger tests in Rehm et al.; Egger P = 0.94 at one to two drinks a day in Roerecke et al.), with little power.

large_effect.note: Relative risks of 5 to 23 at five or more drinks a day in all three sources, including the Danish cohort adjusted for smoking, education and waist size (6.98 in men and 16.2 in women at 28 to 42 drinks a week); the remaining biases (an upward correction of about 1.24 for former drinkers in some studies, confounding by viral hepatitis or obesity, the labelling of cirrhosis as alcoholic) could not plausibly produce differences of this size.

dose_response.note: Risk rises step by step with intake in each source (Table 2 in Rehm et al.; Figure 2 in Roerecke et al.; Fig. 1 in Askgaard et al.).

grade.reasoning: Observational evidence starts low; it is rated down one level each for risk of bias and inconsistency and up one level each for a large effect and a dose–response gradient, which gives low; a strict reading without the upgrades would give very low. Rated as worded: an association that grows with the amount, large at high intake; the claim does not say at what amount the risk begins, because the low-intake estimates conflict. Overlap: the two meta-analyses are by one team and share six studies, and the Danish cohort is one of the newer review's seven cohorts, so they are not three independent confirmations. Status replicated: the independent cohorts shown one by one in the newer review all point the same way at higher intake.
